question: Waste treatment is a key challenge for French Polynesia, a French overseas collectivity with Overseas Country and Territory (OCT) status. Each year, it produces almost 150 000 tonnes of waste, of which less than half is effectively treated. There are several problems with the current waste management system on the islands of French Polynesia.

There is a heavy reliance on landfill (78 % of waste), and the export of recyclable waste is very expensive (200 to 300 million Pacific francs per annum) and has environmental repercussions. Owing to the lack of recycling facilities, recyclable waste is exported. Plastic bottles are shipped from Polynesia to Malaysia; aluminium cans and batteries to South Korea; and paper to Thailand.

In this context, how could the Commission support French Polynesia in developing and implementing more local waste treatment systems? More specifically, are there European funding programmes or technical partnerships that could be used by Polynesia to reduce its waste management carbon footprint, improve sorting and recycling, and reduce the dependency on landfill and recyclable waste exports?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.5.2024) The EU supports financially French Polynesia under Council Decision1 on the association of the Overseas Countries and Territories (OCTs) with the EU including relations between the EU on the one hand, and Greenland and the Kingdom of Denmark on the other (Decision on the Overseas Association, including Greenland).

For 2021-2027, French Polynesia has chosen to focus the EU bilateral cooperation on sustainable water management, that benefits from an EU contribution of EUR 31.1 million. The related programme includes initiatives aligned with waste treatment, notably focusing on waste management from dredging operations.

Under the 11th European Development Fund, the ongoing Pacific OCTs regional programme2, allocating EUR 36 million focuses on sustainable ecosystem management. This programme, running until September 2024, includes specific actions on the reduction and management of diffuse pollution, near water catchment or drilling areas, which can contribute to improving sorting and recycling operations in French Polynesia.

French Polynesia can also participate in other EU programmes on a competitive basis. For example, the BEST 2.0+ programme3 can bring support to local stakeholders in OCTs. By fostering conservation and sustainable practices, the programme indirectly supports the improvement of waste management systems, focusing on reducing environmental impact and enhancing recycling efforts.
Polynesian stakeholders are encouraged to seek additional competitive funding to support their efforts.
